clue.text: Fish-headed hound

parts.note: a hound breed whose name is headed by the name of a fish, a deep-voiced sea perch

explanation.surface: A dog with a face like a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The short-legged scenting dog's name opens with the four-letter fish that shares its spelling with a low singing voice.

clue.text: Bikini results in a charge

parts.note: a toll is a charge paid to use a road or bridge

explanation.surface: Wearing a bikini gets you charged with indecency.
explanation.walkthrough: Bikini is not the swimsuit but the Pacific island where the US tested atom bombs; 'results in' only links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bikini is a ring-shaped coral island in the Marshall Islands, an example of that reef formation.

clue.text: The shape of dirty weather to come …

definitions.text: The shape of dirty weather to come

parts.words: The shape of dirty weather to come
parts.note: a gale warning signal hoisted at coastguard stations was a cone shape, so the shape literally forecasts a storm

explanation.surface: A forecaster warns of grim weather ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis leads into the next clue, whose storm is in a teacup.
explanation.definitionFit: British coastguards hoisted a black canvas cone as a gale signal, its point showing the wind's expected direction.

clue.text: … in this perhaps at five o'clock ?

definitions.text: … in this perhaps at five o'clock ?

parts.words: … in this perhaps at five o'clock ?
parts.note: follows the previous clue's dirty weather: the idiom of a storm in a small vessel for afternoon tea, served at five

explanation.surface: Bad weather brewing at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'storm in a teacup' is a British idiom for a fuss over nothing; five o'clock is the traditional hour for afternoon tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom of a fuss over nothing puts the storm inside a small china vessel used at the afternoon tea table.

clue.text: Where the boffins work out a clue for Othello

definitions.text: Where the boffins work out a clue for Othello

parts.words: Where the boffins work out a clue for Othello
parts.note: a place where research scientists labour, which split in two also reads as an instruction to turn the Moor round

explanation.surface: Scientists puzzle over a hint about Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, 'back' and 'room': ROOM is MOOR backwards, and Othello is the Moor of Venice. 'out' links. Boffins are British slang for research scientists.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret research laboratory where government scientists worked during the war became known by this term for a rear chamber.

clue.text: Classic example of retirement bringing everyone to a size

definitions.text: Classic example of retirement bringing everyone to a size

parts.words: Classic example of retirement bringing everyone to a size
parts.note: in Greek myth a robber made guests lie on his couch, stretching or lopping them to fit it; retiring means going to bed

explanation.surface: A notable case of people standing down so everyone is made the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retirement' means going to bed, not leaving work; 'Classic' points to the Greek classics, where the bandit Procrustes forced travellers to fit his bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase stands for any scheme forcing uniformity, from the Attic robber who stretched or cut his victims to fit.

clue.text: From California a blow pipe

parts.note: a bash is a heavy blow

explanation.surface: A peashooter imported from the West Coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tobacco pipe with a large curved bowl made from a gourd, as smoked by Sherlock Holmes on stage.

clue.text: Bird of devouring appetite ?

parts.note: the name of a large black crow is also a verb meaning to eat greedily

explanation.surface: A greedy bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The big crow's name doubles as a verb for wolfing food, hence ravenous for very hungry.

clue.text: Peers love to ignore the alarm

annotationWithheld.why: Peers love to ignore the alarm (9): OVERSLEEP is an anagram of PEERS LOVE, but no clue word signals the rearrangement; only 'to' is spare, which is not an anagram indicator
annotationWithheld.clue: Peers love to ignore the alarm

clue.text: It takes care of the classic type of the Spanish coast

parts.note: c/o, written CO, is the address abbreviation for care of
roman is the classic upright typeface, as opposed to italic
del is Spanish for of the

explanation.surface: Someone looks after an old printing font from Spain's shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It takes' only links the pieces; 'classic type' is the printer's roman face, not a classical person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Coromandel Coast is the south-eastern shore of India.

clue.text: Always turn the head to change direction

indicators.note: the two letters at the head of the word swap places, as if the head were turned round

parts.note: ever means always

explanation.surface: Keep looking round to alter course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn the head' swaps the first two letters of EVER, giving VEER.
explanation.definitionFit: To swerve or alter course suddenly.

clue.text: No Christmas pie for J. Horner, but equally rewarding

definitions.text: No Christmas pie for J. Horner, but equally rewarding

parts.words: No Christmas pie for J. Horner, but equally rewarding
parts.note: the nursery rhyme boy pulled a fruit out of his Christmas pie; a boiled suet pudding studded with dried fruit holds the same prize

explanation.surface: A rhyme-book boy gets a different treat that pays off just as well.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Little Jack Horner 'put in his thumb, and pulled out a plum'. Plum duff is an old British suet pudding with raisins.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiled suet pudding with raisins, so it holds fruit to pull out just as the rhyme's pie did.

clue.text: Unemployed bishop takes in an exile

indicators.note: takes in means one piece holds another inside it
op is short for opus, a work, so unemployed tells you to take that word for work out

explanation.surface: A jobless clergyman shelters a deportee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unemployed' means out of work: OP (opus, a work) leaves the clergyman's title, and 'takes in' then holds the article. 'exile' is the verb, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To exile someone is to send them away from their country, a verb sense.

clue.text: Nothing remote about this game

parts.note: far means remote, distant
O is the round zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A game with nothing obscure about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about this' links the wordplay to the definition; the pieces join in answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: Faro is an old gambling card game in which players bet on the order cards are dealt.

clue.text: Unable to care less

parts.note: built on the phrase couldn't care less, describing total lack of interest

explanation.surface: Someone who couldn't care less.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone listless and without interest or concern is in a state where nothing could matter less to them.

clue.text: About to take a relative as one of the defence

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for about, concerning
a sister is a relative

explanation.surface: About to adopt a family member as part of a legal defence team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take' links the pieces; 'defence' is resistance, not a court or football back line.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who resists is one of those opposing an attack.

clue.text: Its first may be the last for Partridge

definitions.text: Its first may be the last for Partridge

parts.words: Its first may be the last for Partridge
parts.note: the grouse-and-game shooting season for this bird opens on the first day of a certain month, the day it may be shot

explanation.surface: Someone called Partridge meets their end on the first day of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes Partridge look like a person's name; it is the game bird, whose shooting season in Britain opens on 1 September.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth month opens the British partridge-shooting season on its first day.

clue.text: Like a reformed crook ?

parts.note: a crook is also a bend, and a criminal who goes honest is said to go a certain way that also means unbent

explanation.surface: A criminal turned honest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bend made level is no longer curved, and a criminal gone honest is slang for not bent.

clue.text: Like King James troubled with a nervous affliction

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: a tic is a nervous twitch

explanation.surface: A Stuart king suffering from a twitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges JAMES to MAJES; 'with' joins TIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Regal grandeur, the stately dignity of a monarch.

clue.text: Maker of music for dreams?

parts.note: a wind instrument that plays tunes, and also what an opium smoker uses to bring on visions

explanation.surface: Who writes the soundtrack to our sleep?
explanation.definitionFit: A wind instrument plays music, and a smoker's bowl of opium gives rise to fanciful hopes.

clue.text: Influenced Bob and Edward to get out of the way

indicators.note: out of read as outside: the two names stand on the outside of the road

parts.note: a bob was the old shilling, abbreviated s
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Two men persuaded to step aside.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob was slang for a shilling, written s in old British money. 'out of' means outside: the coin and the name surround the road; 'and' and 'to get' link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be swayed is to be persuaded or moved by argument.

clue.text: Such a charming bit of rhythm !

indicators.note: a bit of the preceding words is taken, letters running across the word breaks

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a delightful dance beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'suCH A CHArming'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin American dance and its rhythm, with a triple step.

clue.text: One that has difficulty threading a needle

definitions.text: One that has difficulty threading a needle

parts.words: One that has difficulty threading a needle
parts.note: from the Gospel saying that it is easier for this desert beast to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter heaven

explanation.surface: Someone with poor eyesight struggles at sewing.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Gospels, Jesus says this desert animal could go through a needle's eye more easily than a rich man into heaven.

clue.text: Hard to handle, being duly fuddled with wine

indicators.note: fuddled means muddled by drink, so these letters are confused

explanation.surface: A person grows awkward when properly tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' and 'with' link; 'fuddled' rearranges DULY and WINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Awkward and cumbersome, difficult to manage.

clue.text: Pennygold is her name

parts.note: split as penny, the old d from the Latin denarius, then gold, or in heraldry
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman introduced by her double-barrelled surname.
explanation.walkthrough: Pennygold looks like a surname; split it into penny (d, from the Latin denarius in old British money) and gold (or).
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, the clue's 'her name'.

clue.text: The little matter of the first half of the alphabet

definitions.text: The little matter of the first half of the alphabet

parts.words: The little matter of the first half of the alphabet
parts.note: a tiny particle of matter, whose name splits as the span of letters from the first to the thirteenth

explanation.surface: A small issue concerning half the letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the first half of the alphabet as 'A to M' and close up the gaps: the result is the smallest unit of matter.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest particle of matter, a tiny piece of a chemical element.

clue.text: A Lincoln address

parts.note: reads as a street address in Lincoln, but is the famous speech the US president gave at a Civil War battlefield in 1863

explanation.surface: Somewhere to live in the English city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln is also an English cathedral city, so 'address' first suggests a house there.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Lincoln's most famous speech was delivered at the Pennsylvania battlefield cemetery that gives it its name.

clue.text: Bill has ring style that's confounded some servicemen

parts.note: ac, short for account, is a bill
O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: confounded means mixed up, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A bill from a ring with a muddled style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'that's' link; 'confounded' rearranges STYLE to LYTES. 'some' links the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Altar assistants who help the priest during a church service.

clue.text: Costume includes the universal mailed fist

indicators.note: includes means one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: dress means costume
U is the British film rating for universal, suitable for all

explanation.surface: An outfit featuring an armoured glove.
explanation.definitionFit: The mailed fist is a figure for force or threats, coercion by violence.
